synopsis: The corpus recommends transferring collision-mitigation settings across machines through physics-based zones using speed, latency, braking deceleration, sensor pose and machine envelope, rather than copying constants [f138, f6681]. At 5–15 km/h, latency can account for half or more of stopping distance; an engineering example adds 22.2 m before braking for a two-second combined operator and mechanical delay at 40 km/h, but this is not a measured reaction time or collision-speed distribution [f144, f5898, f3220]. Grade and payload can change available deceleration by an amount comparable to deceleration itself, so validation must include machine-state factors and cannot establish avoidance with incorrect simulated terrain-dependent deceleration and pitch [f145, f5900, f5819, f3972]. Vendor operating envelopes are narrow: Volvo CE's January 2023 system operates only in reverse at 3–15 km/h and brakes for 2–3 seconds, while Komatsu's stop function acts only at slow travel speeds or the start of motion; the cited Freightliner tests also show that higher-speed success does not imply lower-speed success [f1238, f10439, f1330]. Detection range must support stopping at the operating speed: dust may require slower driving, lidar positioning error increased by up to 27% with speed in one study, and fidelity for real mining dust remains uncertain [f11330, f4705, f5064]. Planning gaps include the absence of an identified collision-speed distribution and an identified test facility or target supplier capable of handling 50–400 t machines at representative speeds; validity records should explicitly bound speed, acceleration, deceleration, brake timing and friction [f3216, f1166, f8010].
